context: Apart Research Swarm Alignment hackathon, tracks 'Science of Agent Networks' and 'Multi-Agent Oversight and Control'. Deadline 2026-11-08 23:59 AoE (~1.5 days, solo, AI-assisted). Resources: one 16 GB GPU (Gemma 3 4B + Gemma Scope 2 SAEs feasible; 12B not at full precision); ~$1,500 Adaption API credits for hosted open-weight models only (deepseek-v4-flash, qwen3.8-27b, gemma-4-31b-it, gemma-4-26b-a4b-it, glm-53-flash, glm-5.2, qwen3.5-397b), cheap enough for thousands of agent episodes. Datasets available: Swarm Traces, AI Village transcripts, METR Hugging Face incident report. Researcher's interest: why agents in seemingly neutral swarms come to propose or accept norm violations, explained game-theoretically and/or mechanistically; conceptual novelty is the priority.
known_failure_modes: Unfalsifiable framing: a thesis where every outcome confirms it (e.g. 'context can override rules').
Bundled manipulations: a single contrast that cannot separate rival explanations (information vs permission vs detection vs wording vs length).
Circular interpretability: a direction built from the same contrast it is then used to explain or steer.
Probe reads the request/scenario, not the hidden variable (rule blindness, arXiv:2608.16852).
Decodable is not causal: steering vectors that predict but don't control; interchangeable vectors (arXiv:2610.19359).
Single-agent work relabelled as swarm research: 'peer' is just a string in one prompt.
Effect exists in few models (fine-as-price: 2 of 10 models in Wired Partners); 4B models may not show it.
Fine-tuning arms that cannot be done credibly in 1.5 days or whose result is already known (fine-tuning reroutes rather than rewrites).
Comparing effect sizes across studies with different models, tasks and baselines.
Claims of novelty for behaviour already published (Okamoto et al. arXiv:2608.12323; Wired Partners; Check Point Oct 2026; Shi et al. arXiv:2609.24967).

cards.claim: The fine-as-price flip is not about price: it decomposes into detection, permission, information and wording components, and in most models detection ('nobody checks') explains most of it.
cards.mechanism: Stated sanctions bundle several signals; models respond to enforcement expectation more than to penalty magnitude.
cards.prediction: At fixed gain and certain detection, acceptance is flat across fine sizes 0.01x-100x gain; 'nobody checks' alone reproduces >=70% of the small-fine effect.
cards.falsifier: Acceptance falls monotonically with fine size at certain detection, tracking g > F.
cards.experiment: Single-decision prompts on 7 Adaption models + Gemma 3 4B: fine-size sweep at fixed gain, plus unspecified penalty, nobody-checks, fee vs fine, irrelevant number, length-matched filler; 50 templates x conditions.
cards.swarm_link: Peers in swarms routinely transmit enforcement beliefs; knowing which component carries the effect says which peer messages are dangerous.

cards.claim: Pricing a rule does not break it; it makes it negotiable: a stated small fine and peer pressure interact super-additively.
cards.mechanism: A fine converts a categorical constraint into a tradeoff, which pressure can then tip; without the fine, pressure triggers categorical defence.
cards.prediction: In a 2x2 (fine x peer pressure), violation(fine+pressure) - baseline > [violation(fine) - baseline] + [violation(pressure) - baseline].
cards.falsifier: Effects are additive or sub-additive across models.
cards.experiment: 2x2 with model-written peer pressure messages from a second hosted model, plus no-message control, across 7 Adaption models; seed from Okamoto's GPT-OSS 94%->14% observation.
cards.swarm_link: Division of labour in rule erosion: one agent prices, another pressures; neither alone suffices.

cards.claim: A stated fine overrides rather than erases the model's internal rule signal.
cards.mechanism: Fine-tuning and prompting usually reroute around existing representations rather than delete them.
cards.prediction: A 'forbidden' direction derived from fine-free prompts stays equally active when a fine is added, while the accept logit rises.
cards.falsifier: The forbidden-direction projection drops in proportion to the acceptance increase.
cards.experiment: Gemma 3 4B, pre-registered layer/token, direction from forbidden vs permitted harmless prompts without fines, controls against refusal and random directions.
cards.swarm_link: If the signal persists, an oversight probe could still detect 'knowingly priced' violations from a monitored agent.

cards.claim: [KILLED - negative example] Rules fall to quiet reframing, not to persuasion.
cards.mechanism: Argument triggers categorical defence; price mention silently switches mode.
cards.prediction: Argument lowers violations; fine mention raises them.
kill_reasons: Persuasive jailbreaks succeed >92% (Zeng et al. 2024); urgency pressure drives compliance to 0% in 10/12 models (Okamoto). Check Point backfire is one model, one scenario.
Built by comparing effect sizes across incomparable studies.

cards.claim: [KILLED - negative example] Fine-tuning a model to treat fines as prices causes broad emergent misalignment.
cards.mechanism: Narrow rule-breaking training generalizes via a persona direction.
kill_reasons: Standard template; Gemma shows ~0.7% EM; rational framing acts like inoculation; not credible in 1.5 days with one seed.
